title: Attention Is All You Need
headline: A model that reads every word in a sentence at the same time by letting each word weigh every other word, replacing the slow step-by-step reading that came before.
abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

images.alt: A row of pixel-art word tiles sit around a round table, one tile glowing clay-orange while thin ink lines of different thickness fan out from it to every other tile, thickest to the words it cares about most, showing that each word weighs every other word at once.
images.caption: Every word weighs every other word at once, and listens hardest to the ones that matter.

images.alt: On the left a single tall clay-orange bar towers over tiny flattened bars while on the right a row of balanced sage bars stands evenly, with a small dial between them marking the scaling step, showing that dividing the scores keeps attention from collapsing onto one word.
images.caption: Without the divide-by-root-d step, big scores collapse the weight onto one word; scaling spreads it back out.

images.alt: The sentence 'the cat sat on the mat' as pixel word tiles, with three translucent lenses laid over it in different tones, each lens tracing its own pattern of curved arcs between words, showing that several attention heads read the same sentence through different lenses at once.
images.caption: Several heads read the same sentence at once, each catching a different kind of link between words.

images.alt: Three pixel word tiles labelled every, word, arrives sit above a sine and cosine wave ribbon that touches each tile with a numbered clay-orange stamp, showing that because the words arrive all at once each one gets a wave-shaped position stamp so order is never lost.
images.caption: Words arrive all at once, so each gets a wave-shaped stamp that marks where it sits in line.
